title: Moving the shorter wall inward
summary: Moving the shorter wall inward can raise container height and increase capacity—here from 21 to 24.
context: In height array ht = [3, 8, 5, 2, 7, 7, 3, 4] (indices 0 to 7), container capacity is cap[i, j] = min(ht[i], ht[j]) × (j - i).
Contrasting with Figure 15-9, which moved the taller wall inward from [0, 7], this figure moves the left shorter-wall pointer rightward from the same starting pair (heights 3 and 4, capacity 21).
description: Right pointer j stays at 7 (height 4) while left pointer i moves right from 0 to 1 (height ht[1] = 8, returning wall 0 to unselected gray). Because left wall 8 now exceeds right wall 4, right wall j = 7 becomes the new shorter wall; the light-blue water region spans indices 1 to 7 at height 4, captioned below "Moving the shorter wall inward may increase capacity" with the current capacity formula.

frames.title: Moving the shorter wall inward
frames.explanation: Width shrinks from 7 to 6 while water height rises from 3 to 4, giving cap = min(8, 4) × (7 - 1) = 24. Moving the shorter wall inward can therefore increase capacity, though not on every step. Capacity 24 is still not the global maximum; Figure 15-7 shows the optimal pair [1, 5] with capacity 28.
